newsitem.title: CANADA: Americans arrested in salmon dispute with Canada.
newsitem.headline: Americans arrested in salmon dispute with Canada.

text.p: Four U.S. fishermen were arrested on Sunday for illegally fishing sockeye salmon in Canadian waters, and their boats, nets and catch were seized, the federal government said.

An official of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans told Reuters the Lynde E and the Wanda Mae were captured in the waters of Juan de Fuca Strait near the city of Victoria off the coast of Vancouver Island while fishing with illegal nets and without the right to fish in Canadian waters.
"The big issue is that they were fishing illegally in our waters," said Robert Martinolich, the department's director of conservation and protection for the Pacific region.

Martinolich said the four fishermen had their boats, nets and catch seized and could face up to C$100,000 (US$72,600) in fines, the loss of the seized items and imprisonment if convicted of illegal fishing.
"They will probably go before a judge tomorrow," Martinolich said, adding that officers who arrested the four men believed the American fishermen knew they were illegally fishing in Canadian waters.

The arrests came amid a dispute between Canada and the United States over salmon fishing that resulted in the blockade of an Alaskan ferry on Saturday by angry Canadian fishermen in Prince Rupert, British Columbia.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corp. reported on Sunday that the ferry operator, Alaska Marine Highway, had obtained a court order demanding the fishermen disband their blockade. It said a convoy of trucks also detained by angry fishermen had obtained a court order to allow passage through a roadblock.
CBC reported the trucks had been allowed to pass on Sunday but the blockaded ferry was still unable to leave port.

Bob King, press secretary to Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles, said in Juneau, Alaska: "The fishermen have indicated that they don't intend to abide by the court order. Neither thave we seen any willingness of law enforcement to enforce this court order."

By Sunday, King said, about 100 of more than 300 passengers remained on the Malaspina, the blockaded ferry. The state gave refunds to passengers who departed and was trying to arrange alternative transportation for them, he said.
"The passengers are just being used as pawns in this, which we think is totally wrong," King said.
On Saturday Knowles suspended regular state ferry service to Prince Rupert.
King said Alaska was considering ending its contract to operate a terminal in the Canadian port.
"If we can't assure them safe passage into Prince Rupert, we're not going to take them there. So why do we need a terminal? It's not a threat; it's common sense," he said.
He rejected Canadian claims that Alaskans were overfishing sockeye.
"We're managing the Noyes Island fishery based on pink salmon abundance, and we feel we're conducting this fishery in accordance with the Pacific Salmon Treaty," he said.
Pink salmon are very abundant in Alaska waters, so more than the normal amount of sockeye (also called red) salmon are being taken incidentally in the catch, he said.
"But we've taken steps to reduce this interception, steps that have been successful," he said.
The issue was nearly resolved in the "stakeholder" negotiations held over the winter, with concessions offered by the Alaskans, but the Canadian government broke off those talks, King said.
Alaska wants the stakeholder talks to resume in the fall, he said. "But we're not going to be negotiating fishing matters when they're holding one of our state ferries hostage," he said.
